Tycho dies; Kepler closes the observation journal with the account of his illness and death.

The Emperor secures the observations and instruments from the heirs, who had asked 100,000 thalers, for 20,000 at six per cent; 4,000 are paid in 1602 and 1,000 in 1608, and nothing after. The claim was still unsettled in 1671.

An imperial order to Kepler to pack the instruments and send them to Vienna 'for greater safety'; apparently not carried out.

Destruction in the disturbances that followed the death of Emperor Matthias, when Prague was held for Frederick of the Palatinate: some instruments converted to other uses, the rest destroyed or dispersed (Gassendi, Vita, 1655, p. 216). The version that attaches the loss to the battle of the White Mountain, 8 November 1620, is a misreading of Gassendi.
The inventory of the Prague treasury and Kunstkammer still lists, in the Belvedere, 'no. 1424, a very large celestial globe of metal' and 'no. 1425, a quadrant with many appurtenant instruments'.

The globe is acquired by Christoph Scheiner for the Jesuit college at Neisse in Silesia.
Prince Ulrik, son of Christian IV, takes the globe from Neisse as war booty to Copenhagen, where it is placed in the observatory of the Round Tower.

The globe burns in the Round Tower fire; the wooden body is consumed and the brass melts, leaving some lumps, the meridian ring, iron rings and the axle, since lost.

The Prague observatory's earliest inventory lists 'No. 4, a large sextant of Tycho Brahe, made in the year 1600 by Erasmus Habermel' and 'No. 5, a smaller sextant of Tycho Brahe, which he brought with him to Prague'.
At Joseph II's auction of the Castle collections the two sextants are sold to Franz Leonard Herget, public teacher of mechanics and hydraulics.
